title: Agent Visibility vs. Agent Governance
summary: Observing an agent's action and controlling it are two different systems. Where monitoring stops, where the enforcement point sits, what the EU AI Act demands after the December 2027 delay, and how each half fails alone.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**Most "governance programs" turn out to be visibility with a written rule stapled to the front, and the size of the gap is now measurable rather than anecdotal.**


Palo Alto Networks' 2026 Identity Security Landscape, a survey of more than 2,900 security decision-makers, puts machine identities at 109 per human in the enterprise, up from 82:1 the year before. Among the organizations running agents, it reports that "only 37% can revoke an AI agent's credentials" and "only 30% have immutable audit logging for what those agents do."


The common reading is that watching is the hard part. It isn't. Observation is what vendors sell and what actually ships. The decision about what an agent may do, wired to something capable of stopping it, is the part that stays on a slide.


We are not arguing that visibility is wasted money. NIST's zero trust tenets put continuous collection at the centre of the architecture, and nobody can compare behaviour against a rule they cannot see. Visibility is a precondition that keeps getting mistaken for the finish line.


What to do today: take one agent, write down the single action it must never perform, and go find the code that would stop it. If that code does not exist, what you have is visibility.
